newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Time may work against Portugal on E.Timor issue.
newsitem.headline: Time may work against Portugal on E.Timor issue.

text.p: Time may be running out for Lisbon to reach an agreement with Jakarta on the future of East Timor, the former Portuguese colony annexed by Indonesia two decades ago, political and diplomatic analysts say.
The East Timor question is unlikely to be answered while President Suharto, Indonesia's ruler for the past 30 years, remains in power, some diplomats and analysts have said.

But official Indonesian sources said that Portugal could be mistaken if it hopes to secure a deal by holding out until Suharto -- who is 75 and is expected to seek a seventh five-year term in power in 1998 -- has left the scene.
"Things will change after President Suharto, but if there is a change, it may be much harder (to resolve the issue)," one source said.
"We think the Portuguese think that a change will make it easier. But it's not going to be like that," he added.
Indonesian troops invaded East Timor in December 1975 with tacit Western support after civil war broke out following the abrupt withdrawal of Portuguese colonial authorities.

Indonesia incorporated the territory as its 27th province the following July in a move the United Nations has refused to recognise. Jakarta has since sought to stamp out a lingering East Timorese independence movement.
Human rights groups estimate about 200,000 people have died in the invasion, subsequent famine and other unrest in the past two decades.
U.N.-sponsored talks between Indonesia and Portugal on reaching an internationally acceptable solution to East Timor's future have dragged on for nearly 15 years.

Portugal supports demands by East Timor resistance leaders that the territory's people be allowed to decide their own future. But Jakarta says a 1976 vote vote showed support to become part of Indonesia.
Some analysts said a solution to issues surrounding East Timor appears increasingly needed.
The U.N. special envoy on East Timor, Jamsheed Marker, visited the territory this weekend. He said earlier this month in Lisbon that he hoped to speed up talks on the issue.

"This is not just a small problem, but a major problem for countries in the region," said a senior diplomat in the Asian region. "The solution is some type of autonomy, but there is a lack of ways to achieve this."
"It suits the interests of hard-liners in Portugal and Indonesia to continue the standoff, the moderates are very thinly spread," he added.

John Shattuck, U.S. Assistant Secretary of State for democracy, human rights and labour, also said at the end of a 24-hour visit to East Timor's capital Dili on Friday there was an urgent need for dialogue on the territory to move forward.
Official Indonesian sources say there is no question of Jakarta relinquishing sovereignty over East Timor, a mainly-Catholic territory of some 850,000 people.
The problem is to find a form of government acceptable to all sides.

The Indonesian sources said Suharto, who was the nation's leader at the time of the Indonesian invasion, reacts like a bull to a red flag when he hears the term "autonomy" and has rejected several proposals.
"If they can find some way of not using the term autonomy, and instead use something like 'special region', that might be the solution," one source said.

He noted that Indonesia had granted nominal special region status to areas such as Aceh in northern Sumatra and Yogyakarta, Indonesia's one-time capital on the main island of Java, for historical and ethnic reasons.
East Timor's co-recipient of the 1996 Nobel Peace Prize, Catholic Bishop Carlos Belo, told Reuters on Thursday some measure of autonomy was needed for the territory.
"Timor is different culturally, historically from other parts of Indonesia. Give some concession, let the people have their autonomy," he said.

Diplomatic sources said Portugal's hard line on the issue was alienating other countries, including members of the European Union whose desire for stronger political and economic ties with Southeast Asia were being thwarted by Lisbon over East Timor.
